content: Heparin sodium is prescribed to prevent the formation of blood clots in individuals with certain medical conditions or those undergoing medical procedures that increase the risk of clot formation. It is also used to stop the growth of existing blood clots in blood vessels, although it cannot reduce the size of clots that have already formed. Additionally, heparin is used in small amounts to prevent blood clots from forming in catheters, which are small plastic tubes inserted into veins for administering medication or drawing blood over time. Heparin belongs to a class of medications called anticoagulants, commonly referred to as blood thinners. It works by reducing the blood's ability to clot. Heparin is available as a liquid solution for injection either intravenously (into a vein) or subcutaneously (deeply under the skin). It is also available as a diluted solution for injection into intravenous catheters. Heparin should never be injected into a muscle. Depending on the condition being treated, heparin may be administered one to six times daily or as a slow, continuous intravenous infusion. When used to prevent blood clots in intravenous catheters, it is typically administered when the catheter is first placed and each time blood is drawn or medication is given through the catheter. Heparin may be administered by a nurse or healthcare provider, or you may be instructed to inject it yourself at home. If you are self-administering heparin, a healthcare provider will demonstrate the proper technique. If you have any questions about where to inject the medication, how to administer it, or how to dispose of used needles and syringes, consult your doctor, nurse, or pharmacist. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and do not use more or less of the medication or use it more frequently than prescribed. Heparin solutions come in different strengths, and using the wrong strength can lead to serious complications. Always check the package label to ensure you are using the correct strength prescribed by your doctor. If the strength is incorrect, do not use the medication and contact your doctor or pharmacist immediately. Your doctor may adjust your dose during treatment, so ensure you understand the exact amount of medication you need to use. Heparin is sometimes used alone or in combination with aspirin to prevent pregnancy loss and other complications in pregnant women with certain medical conditions who have experienced these issues in previous pregnancies. Discuss the risks of using this medication with your doctor or pharmacist. Heparin may also be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before using heparin, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to heparin, any other medications, beef or pork products, or any ingredients in heparin injections. Ask your healthcare provider for a list of ingredients if needed. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are taking or plan to take. Be sure to mention anticoagulants like warfarin, antihistamines, aspirin or aspirin-containing products, NSAIDs like ibuprofen or naproxen, digoxin, dipyridamole, hydroxychloroquine, indomethacin, quinine, tetracycline antibiotics, and any other relevant medications. Your doctor may need to adjust your doses or monitor you closely for side effects. Inform your doctor if you have a low platelet count, heavy bleeding that cannot be stopped, or if you are currently menstruating. Also, let your doctor know if you have a fever, infection, or have recently undergone a spinal tap, spinal anesthesia, surgery (especially involving the brain, spinal cord, or eyes), or a heart attack. Additionally, disclose if you have or have ever had a bleeding disorder, blood clots, unusual bruising, cancer, stomach or intestinal ulcers, high blood pressure, or liver disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while using heparin, contact your doctor immediately. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental surgery, inform your healthcare provider that you are using heparin. Smoking may reduce the effectiveness of this medication, so inform your doctor if you smoke or have recently quit. Unless otherwise directed by your doctor, continue your normal diet while using heparin. If you forget to inject a dose, consult your doctor for guidance on what to do. Heparin may cause side effects. Common side effects include redness, pain, bruising, or sores at the injection site, as well as hair loss. Serious side effects include unusual bruising or bleeding, blood in vomit or stool, black or tarry stools, blood in urine, excessive tiredness, nausea, vomiting, chest pain, coughing up blood, severe headache, lightheadedness, sudden loss of balance, numbness or weakness on one side of the body, difficulty speaking or understanding speech, vision problems, purple or black skin discoloration, pain and discoloration in the arms or legs, itching or burning (especially on the feet), chills, fever, hives, rash, wheezing, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing or swallowing, hoarseness, or painful erections lasting for hours. Heparin may also cause osteoporosis, particularly with long-term use. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience any of these symptoms or other unusual problems while using this medication. If you are injecting heparin at home, your healthcare provider will provide storage instructions. Keep the medication in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Store it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture, and do not freeze it. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for disposal instructions. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call 911. Symptoms of overdose may include nosebleeds, blood in urine, black or tarry stools, easy bruising, unusual bleeding, red blood in stools, or blood in vomit that resembles coffee grounds. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory for monitoring. Your doctor may order tests to evaluate your response to heparin and may ask you to check your stool for blood using an at-home test. Inform all healthcare providers and laboratory personnel that you are using heparin before undergoing any tests. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription. Maintain a written list of all medications, supplements, and vitamins you are taking, and bring this list to all medical appointments or hospital visits. This information is also crucial in emergencies.
